newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chinese flags fly, briefly, over Japan-held isles.
newsitem.headline: Chinese flags fly, briefly, over Japan-held isles.

text.p: Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon on Monday, swam ashore and hoisted Chinese flags on an East China Sea island chain, boldly challenging Japan's claim of sovereignty.

Frogmen scrambled through rough surf in a dawn landing on one of the isles to hoist the red five-star of the communist People's Republic of China and the rival blue-and-red flag of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China.
Some 300 protesters aboard a 50-boat flotilla vying to claim the chain back for one or the other of the rival Chinas let up a great roar of approval as the flags whipped against a blue sky.
The image was fleeting, however, as blustery winds soon sent the flags tumbling into the water. A separate landing on another shore was similarly brief.
At least two demonstrators who fell overboard during the excitement were rescued.
Protest leaders quickly withdrew their forces and left the islands, claimed by Japan since 1895 as the Senkakus and by China and Taiwan as the Diaoyus. But they pledged to return.
"We will continue our effort to protect the Diaoyus and to retake the Diaoyus," Taiwan protest organiser Chin Chieh-shou told state radio. "We will not quit until we succeed."

Mission leaders failed to remove a lighthouse erected on the islands by Japanese rightists in July, a move to assert Tokyo's claim that sparked anti-Japanese and increasingly nationalist protests among Chinese in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and China.
Japan lamented what it called the illegal landing and would not rule out arresting future landing parties, saying its fleet of 60 maritime safety boats had "acted prudently".

"It was very regrettable that protesters from Taiwan and Hong Kong illegally landed on Japan's territory despite repeated warnings to retreat from the islands," government spokesman Teijiro Furukawa said in Tokyo.
"If protesters do act (again), disobeying our warnings, we will take proper measures," he added.
Japanese patrols blasted orders to retreat and jockeyed into the paths of landing craft but were unable to thwart waves of small boats whose crews had spent a week practising landings.
The captain of one of at least three protest boats involved in collisions said a Japanese patrol deliberately butted his stern, causing minor damage. Japan denied the report.
Videotape shot by a Japanese television helicopter showed many collisions between Japanese forces and protest boats in chaotic confrontations just metres (yards) from the rocks.
One protest boat was crippled badly enough in a collision that 13 of its 15 passengers had to be moved to safety to other craft. It was returning to Taiwan under its own steam.

Until Monday, Japan's coastal patrols had managed to repulse all earlier landing attempts -- one of which ended in tragedy on September 26 when Hong Kong protest leader David Chan, whose boat too had been turned away, leapt into a roiling sea to defy Japanese sovereignty. He drowned.

Taiwan maritime police vessels were in the vicinity on Monday but did not interfere. A Taiwan military helicopter entered the area to rescue an ailing protester but failed to find him, Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency reported.
China and Nationalist-ruled Taiwan have been rivals since the end of a civil war in 1949, when the defeated Republic of China government fled into exile on the offshore island.
